extracted.intended_audience: historians, bibliographers, and readers interested in early Anglo‑American history and Thomas Hariot
extracted.subtask_description: A privately printed biographical and bibliographical study of Thomas Hariot and his Report of Virginia, assembled from dormant materials and aimed at recovering and accurately reproducing early Anglo‑American primary sources. The volume includes editorial commentary, selections for reprint, and notes on editorial and publication practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objectives of the Hercules Club
rubrics_metrics.description: "The objects of this Association are literary, social, antiquarian, festive and historical; and its aims are thoroughly independent research into the materials of early Anglo‑American history and literature."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Club's platform is to pursue independent research into early Anglo‑American materials and to clear errors in the historical record; membership is cooperative in spirit though practical editing largely fell to Henry Stevens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection criterion for publication list
rubrics_metrics.description: "The following ten works were selected as the first field of the Club's investigations, and to form the first series of its publications."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preferred items are unique or of the highest rarity and of great historic value; the prospectus lists ten early works (Waymouth, De Bry items, Hariot's Briefe and True Report, etc.) as exemplars of what to pursue and reproduce.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard for reproduction and editorial fidelity
rubrics_metrics.description: "It is one of the purposes therefore of the Hercules Club to ferret out these materials, collate, edit and reproduce them with extreme accuracy, but not in facsimile."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial policy favors careful collation and accurate reproduction of texts (i.e., scholarly editing) rather than issuing photographic facsimiles; emphasis on textual accuracy and editorial collation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Importance of competent editorial oversight
rubrics_metrics.description: "I have from time to time unsuccessfully endeavoured to enlist the services of various editors competent to complete the projected eleven volumes ... but after a lapse of nearly fourteen years I have awakened to the fact that no actual progress has been made..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Projects of this kind require competent, committed editors; reliance on cooperative subscription without dedicated editorial labor leads to delay; practical editorial responsibility often falls to a single capable individual.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication and subscription practice for privately printed works
rubrics_metrics.description: "The two volumes ... are now offered for subscription as privately printed books ... The entire impression consists of 150 copies on small paper, 33 copies on large paper, together with 12 extra ..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedural standards: offer surviving members first refusal, state edition sizes and paper types, describe format differences (small/large paper), and clearly state subscription/allocation order; transparency about limited impressions is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality and craft of printing and binding as a criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: "Few English books of its time, 1588, surpass it either in typographic execution or literary merit. ... The paper is the finest handmade, specially prepared ..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High typographic execution, careful printing and fine paper/binding are considered part of the work's merit when reproducing rare early texts; physical production values are explicitly noted as part of bibliographical importance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value criteria for primary historical authorities
rubrics_metrics.description: Hariot's Report is described as "the first original authority in our language relating to that part of English North America ... so full and trustworthy that almost everything of a primeval character ... may be traced back to it as to a first parent."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Primary documents are judged by originality, trustworthiness, freshness, and comprehensiveness; illustrated accounts (e.g., White's drawings) enhance value; such works serve as foundational authorities for reconstructing early history and culture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement for clear, explicit, contemporary evidence when overturning received opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: "A decision of mankind of two centuries' standing ... cannot be easily reversed without good contemporary evidence. This I have endeavoured to produce."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When challenging long‑standing historical judgments, one must present clear, explicit, and contemporary documentary evidence; the editor/biographer must be cautious and rigorous in argumentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of biographical treatment and inclusion of associates' notices
rubrics_metrics.description: "The book necessarily includes notices, more or less elaborate, of very many of Hariot's friends, associates and contemporaries, while others, for want of space, are mentioned little more than by name."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Biographical works on figures like Hariot should contextualize the subject by including biographical and bibliographical disquisitions on associates; editorial judgment governs depth of individual notices according to space and relevance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Importance of recovering documentary evidence (e.g., wills, MSS.)
rubrics_metrics.description: "All the new documents mentioned have their special value, but too much importance cannot be attached to the recovery of Hariot's Will, for it at once dispels a great deal of the inference and conjecture that have so long beclouded his memory."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discovery and publication of primary documents (wills, letters, manuscripts) are pivotal for resolving historical conjectures and for illuminating a subject's life; editors should prioritize locating such sources.
